how-to-set-multi-window-burn-rate-alerts.text:
SLO Burn-Rate Alerts · GUIDE

How to set multi-window burn-rate alerts for an SLO

A fixed "error rate above 1%" alert pages you for blips and misses slow leaks. Alerting on how fast the error budget is being spent fixes both. This is the method, with the arithmetic, so you can check any generated rule by hand.

1. The budget

A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows 0.1% bad requests. Under a full outage that is 30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes. That number is the budget; everything else is how fast you spend it.

2. The burn rate

A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the whole budget by the end of the period. A burn rate of 14.4 spends it 14.4 times faster, so 2% of the budget goes in one hour. The general formula is burn = fraction x period / window.

SeverityBudget spentLong / short windowBurn rate (30 days)Error ratio at 99.9%
page2%1h / 5m14.41.44%
page5%6h / 30m60.6%
ticket10%1d / 2h30.3%
ticket10%3d / 6h10.1%

3. Why both windows must agree

The alert fires only while the long window and the short window are above the threshold. The long window keeps a brief spike from paging; the short window lets the alert clear within minutes of the fix instead of an hour later.

4. Check it can fire at all

The threshold is burn x (1 - SLO). At a 90% SLO the page threshold is 14.4 x 10% = 144%, and no error ratio exceeds 100%, so that alert can never fire. Low-traffic services have the opposite problem: if the short window expects under one failing request at the threshold, a single error flips it. The generator flags both.

5. Recording rules keep it cheap

Compute sum(rate(errors[W])) / sum(rate(total[W])) once per window as a recording rule, then compare the recorded series to the threshold in the alert. The generator emits seven recordings and four alerts.

Common questions

Where does 14.4 come from?

It is the burn rate at which 2% of a 30-day error budget is spent in one hour: 0.02 x 720 hours / 1 hour = 14.4. For a 28-day period the same policy gives 13.44.

Why two windows?

The long window filters out blips and the short window makes the alert stop firing soon after the problem is fixed. Requiring both gives fast detection with few false pages.

SLO BURN-RATE ALERTS · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

From an SLO to alert rules that actually fire

Type your SLO and get the downtime budget, the multi-window burn-rate thresholds from the Google SRE Workbook, how fast each alert fires in an outage, warnings for thresholds that can never fire, and a Prometheus rules file to review.

Nothing is uploaded. This is arithmetic in your browser on the numbers you type; it never contacts your Prometheus.

Run promtool check rules slo-api.rules.yml and try each expression in your own Prometheus before loading it.

  


  

    
Prefer a CLI?

    
node cli.mjs plan --slo 99.9 --rps 40
node cli.mjs plan --slo 99.9 --json
node cli.mjs rules --slo 99.9 --name api \
  --errors 'http_requests_total{job="api",code=~"5.."}' \
  --total 'http_requests_total{job="api"}' > slo-api.rules.yml

    
Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. plan exits 1 on an unreachable threshold, so it can gate a pull request that edits an SLO. More: how to set multi-window burn-rate alerts for an SLO.

  


  

    
Common questions

    
What is a multi-window, multi-burn-rate alert?

    
Instead of alerting when the error rate crosses a fixed number, you alert on how fast the error budget is being spent. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget exactly at the end of the period; 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. Requiring a long and a short window to both exceed the threshold makes it page quickly on real outages and reset quickly once fixed.

    
Why does my 99% or 90% SLO never alert?

    
The page threshold is the burn rate times the allowed error ratio. For a 90% SLO that is 14.4 x 10% = 144%, which an error ratio cannot reach, so the alert can never fire. The tool flags this and you should lengthen the window or lower the budget fraction.

    
Does this connect to my Prometheus or read my metrics?

    
No. It does arithmetic on the numbers you type and prints a rule file. It never contacts any server and nothing you type is uploaded.

    
Are the generated rules safe to paste into production?

    
Treat them as a reviewed starting point. They assume your error and total selectors are counters you can rate(), that traffic is steady enough for ratio alerts, and that you have tested the expression in your own Prometheus. Run promtool check rules and try the expressions in the expression browser first.
